### page_1
Paleomagnetism of Archean rocks from northwestern Ontario: 
Wabigoon gabbro, Wabigoon Subprovince 
DAVID J. DUNLOP 
Geophysics Laboratory, Department of Physics, University of Toronto, Toronto, Ont., Canada M5S lA7 
Received March 8, 1983 
Revision accepted July 26, 1983 
The Wabigoon gabbro of the Archean Wabigoon greenstone belt in northwestern Ontario preserves a univectorial natural 
remanent magnetization (NRM) with D = 246O, I = 12" (k = 19.5, ag5 = 10.SO, N = 11 sites). The precisionis reduced if sample 
means are averaged, however (k = 9.3, ag5 = 9.2", N = 29 samples). The paleomagnetic pole falls either at 160°W, 11"s 
(6p = 5.3", 6m = 10.6"), corresponding to an age of - 1300 Ma on the Laurentian apparent polar wander path, or tlie reverse of 
this, 20°E, 11" N, corresponding to a late Archean age (-2800 Ma). No -1300 Ma igneous or metamorphic event is 
known in the area; a major west-northwest-trending dike about 9 km south of the gabbro yields a virtual geomagnetic pole at 
122"W, 45"N and seems to be of Abitibi age (-2150 Ma) rather than Mackenzie age (- 1250 Ma). A few gabbro samples and 
some greenstones from the intrusive baked zone have hybrid remanences in which a higher blocking temperature Kenoran-age 
(-2600 Ma) NRM is superimposed on the gabbro characteristic NRM. However, the Kenoran component may be a younger 
chemical remanent magnetization (CRM) residing in hematite. The hypothesis that the gabbro characteristic remanence is itself a 
hybrid of Kenoran and Keweenawan (- 1100 Ma) NRM's, which would explain both the high between-sample scatter and the 
lack of a -1300 Ma remagnetizing event, is considered but rejected because fewer than 10% of the gabbro samples exhibit 
multivectorial swings during alternating field or thermal cleaning. Two geomagnetic field reversals are recorded at interior sites, 
but only one or none is recorded near the margin of the intrusion. The different cooling histories of margin and interior, as well as 
the bulk of the other evidence, favour magnetization during initial cooling in late Archean time.

Can. 1. Earth Sci. 20, 1805-1817 (1983) [Traduit par le journal] 
Introduction 
The "Superior Geotraverse" project was a cooperative 
investigation of the Archean greenstone and gneiss belts 
of the western ~upeiior Province in northwestem Ontario, 
using a combination of geological, geochemical, and 
geophysical methods. A partial report of results appeared 
in 1979 (Canadian Journal of Earth Sciences, Vol. 16, 
No. lo), including a reconnaissance regional paleo- 
magnetic study (Dunlop 1979~). The present paper is 
the first in a series reporting paleomagnetic and rock 
magnetic data for individual formations in and near the 
Superior Geotraverse region. 
The Wabigoon and Shebandowan volcanic-plutonic 
belts in the southern part of the Superior Geotraverse 
area (Fig. la) have been regionally metamorphosed to 
greenschist facies. The regional grade of the intervening 
Quetico gneiss belt is lower amphibolite. The Wabigoon 
gabbro, the subject of this paper, is located in the 
Wabigoon belt just west of the Geotraverse corridor, 
near the village of Wabigoon, Ontario. 
The regional geology of the Dryden-Wabigoon area 
is illustrated in Fig. 1 b. Archean mafic metavolcanics 
and metasediments are intruded by a number of small 
mafic to ultrarnafic bodies, of which the Wabigoon

### page_2
CAN. J. EARTH SCI. VOL. 20, 1983 
FIG. 1. (a) Subprovinces of the Superior Province in central and western Ontario, showing the locations of the Geotraverse area 
and the map area of (b). (b) Regional geology of the Dryden-Wabigoon area, indicating the location of the Wabigoon gabbro and 
sampling sites for the Wabigoon dike ~d the Dyment greenstone. 
gabbro is one example, and by granitic to granodioritic 
stocks and plutons, probably of Kenoran age (-2600 
Ma). 
Dikes are relatively scarce in the western Superior 
Province, but a major west-northwest-trending quartz 
diabase dike crosses the map area just south of Wabigoon 
Lake. It may be continuous with other on-strike dikes to 
the east, paralleling Highway 17 from Ignace to Lac des 
Mille Lacs. Its strike length is at least 70 km, and may be 
as much as 270 km. Although it is mapped as Keweena- 
wan (Satterly 1941), its age is an open question. 
Sampling and measurement procedures 
The Wabigoon dike was sampled at two sites (A and B 
in Fig. 1 b) south of Dryden. South of Dyment, the dike 
could not be located in drift-covered terrain. Green- 
stones near the mapped contact were sampled at a single 
site (A in Fig. 1 b). The Wabigoon gabbro was sampled 
at 11 sites (Fig. 2), and the greenstones it intrudes were 
sampled at two sites (site 2 about 0.25 km from the 
contact, and site 5 very near the contact). A total of 61 
samples of the Wabigoon gabbro and its contact rocks 
and 16 samples of the Wabigoon dike and its contact 
rocks were collected. Three sites were field drilled; at 
the other sites, block samples were taken. The samples 
are not strongly magnetized and orientation by Brunton 
compass was sufficient. 
Two specimens were cut from each drill core and at

### page_3
FIG. 2. Sampling sites in and near the Wabigoon gabbro. 
least three specimens from each block sample. When- 
ever possible, two (sometimes three) specimens were 
alternating field (AF) demagnetized in steps to 1000 Oe 
(0.1 T), using a Schonstedt single-axis AF demagnetizer, 
and one specimen was thermally demagnetized in steps 
to at least 600°C (sometimes to 680°C). Early runs were 
made in a homebuilt furnace with field nulling by 
Helmholtz coils; later runs used a Schonstedt shielded 
furnace. A full program of measurements was carried 
out on each specimen. No blanket cleaning was used. 
Natural remanent magnetization (NRM) measure- 
ments were made with a Digico spinner magnetometer. 
Thermomagnetic curves were measured in a vacuum of 
-10 mTorr (- 1.3 Pa) and a field of -3 kOe (-0.3 T) 
with a recording Curie balance (Bailey 1980). 
Results--Wabigoon gabbro 
Thermomagnetic analysis 
Strong-field, vacuum thermomagnetic curves, of 
which Fig. 3 is a particularly noise-free example, indicate 
that magnetite with a Curie temperature between 550 
and 580°C is the principal magnetic phase. Minor

### page_4
1808 CAN. 1. EARTH SCI. VOL. 20, 1983 
FIG. 3. Vacuum thermomagnetic curve for sample WB 61 
(site 3), indicating nearly pure magnetite as the predominant 
magnetic mineral. 
hematite and possibly also pyrrhotite or maghemite are 
revealed by thermal demagnetization. 
AF demagnetization 
Typical changes in the NRM vector during AF 
demagnetization are shown in the equal-area stereoplots 
of Fig. 4. A relatively soft NRM component approxi- 
mately in the direction of the present Earth's field (PEF) 
is removed by 300-400 Oe (0.03-0.04 T) cleaning. In 
some cases, it is the predominant remanence (e.g., WB 
112, 211, 212, 2212); in others, it is a minor contami- 
nant (e.g., WB 1511, 1611, 16/2,46/1,46/2,46/3). 
The characteristic remanence isolated by AF cleaning 
has south-southwest to west declination and intermediate 
positive to shallow negative inclination (reverse polarity, 
most specimens) or the reverse of this (normal polarity, 
e.g., WB 1811, 1812). The northeast direction is 
arbitrarily designated as normal because it is closest to 
the PEF. 
Directional coherence is reasonably good except in 
rather weakly magnetized samples (NRM emu 
cm-3 A m-I)), which tend to exhibit a cyclic 
displacement of the magnetization vector at higher AF 
levels as the last axis of demagnetization is permuted. 
This "spruce-tree" effect is evident in WB 311, 312, 
1811, 1812, 4611, 4612, and 5211. It seems to be 
sample dependent and not related to instrumental an- 
hysteretic remanences; it can be adequately corrected for 
by vector averaging X-last, Y-last, and 2-last de- 
magnetization results at a given AF level (Zijderveld 
1975). 
Figure 4 shows a few examples of vector swings from 
the characteristic direction towards a south to south- 
southwest direction with shallow negative inclination 
(e.g., WB 1511, 1711, 1912, 3811, 3812). This latter 
direction is well expressed in many units in the Geo- 
traverse region (Dunlop 1979a) and elsewhere in the 
Superior Province (e.g., Schutts and Dunlop 1981). It 
corresponds to a Kenoran age of magnetization (-2600 
Ma). 
AF intensity decay curves for several samples with 
essentially single-component NRM's are given in Fig. 
5. Samples like WB 3/2 that display prominent spruce 
trees (Fig. 4), have soft, rather erratic decay curves. 
Moderately hard characteristic remanences, with median 
destructive fields (MDF's) 3400 Oe (0.04 T), are more 
typical of the collection (e.g., WB 1812, 2211). (The 
initial dip and recovery in the decay data for 1812 are 
due to the elimination of a soft PEF remanence.) 
Thermal demagnetization 
Changes in the NRM vector during thermal demagnetiza- 
tion (Fig. 6) are generally similar to changes in AF 
cleaning. Initial PEF components are frequent (e.g., 
WB 214, 1614) and, with the single exception of 214, 
have blocking temperatures (TB's) 5 305"C, as expected 
for viscous overprinting at ordinary temperatures (Wilson 
and Smith 1968; Dunlop 1969). 
The characteristic remanence is usually isolated 
between 305 and 575"C, but is occasionall; stable to 
625°C (e.g., WB 1614, 2614). Both polarities are 
found, normal (N) being less common than reversed 
(R). Hybrid or bivectorial remanences (N or R charac- 
teristic + Kenoran) are rare. In only two cases, WB 2114 
and 3813, did the NRM vector stabilize at a southward 
negative-inclination direction. The NRM vectors of two 
contact rocks, WB 17/4 and 1914, began to migrate 
southward at low temperatures, but the swings were 
short compared with the corresponding AF swings (WB 
1711, 1912 in Fig. 4). 
Magnetization reversals 
Reversals of magnetization (usually R + N) in 
individual specimens were frequently observed during 
thermal cleaning. They were never observed in AF 
cleaning. Most reversals were close to 180" (e.g., WB 
1614, 21 14, 2614 in Fig. 6), but a few were distinctly 
less than 180" (e.g., 1914, 2914). Of the 22 samples 
from sites 4- 1 1 and 13 that behaved stably during 
thermal demagnetization, 1 1 underwent complete rever- 
sals and a further 8 began swings but dropped into the 
noise level before completing a reversal. 
The observed reversals could have one of several i 
causes: (1) reversal of the geomagnetic field during 
cooling (following intrusion or during later regional 
uplift); (2) self-reversal of themoremanent magnetiza- 
tion (TRM) during cooling; or (3) overprinting of TRM 
by a reversed chemical remanence (CRM). The first 
possibility is the most likely, as the following discussion 
will show. If either field reversal or self-reversal 
occurred, the R and N remanences should occupy

FIG. 5. Representative AF intensity decay curves for

non-overlapping parts of the TB spectrum. CRM over- 
printing may overlap the TB spectrum of the residual 
TRM, although it does not invariably do so. 
Non-overlapping TB spectra of R and N remanences 
are in fact typical of the Wabigoon collection. Figure 7 
gives examples of Zijderveld (1967) plots, or Z-plots, in 
which matching straight-line segments in both horizontal- 
plane and vertical-plane projections represent separate 
NRM components whose TB spectra do not overlap 
(Dunlop 1979b). The temperature at which linear seg- 
ments representing R and N components intersect is the 
reversal temperature. It is quite sharp for all the 
specimens illustrated. (In the case of WB 214, thermo- 
viscous overprinting of an R characteristic is recorded, 
rather than an R + N composite.) 
The behaviour of WB 1614 is representative of 
practically all gabbro samples taken at or near the 
margin of the intrusion (sites 4, 6, 9, 10, and 13). The 
NRM vector begins to migrate towards an N orientation 
above 350-400°C (Fig. 6; cf. also WB 2114, site 6). 
However, the Z-plot shows that between 305 and 575°C 
only the R magnetization is being removed. The N 
magnetization is confined to the TB range above 575°C 
and is presumably carried by hematite. Notice that the 
NRM vector of WB 21 14, after apparently stabilizing in 
a Kenoran direction between 500 and 560°C, likewise 
completes a reversal at 580-600°C (Fig. 6). 
Although the R and N remanence in these samples 
occupy mutually exclusive TB ranges, it is not possible

### page_6
CAN. J. EARTH SCI. VOL. 20, 1983 
FIG. 6. Equal-area projections of thermally cleaned vector NRM data for the Wabigoon gabbro. Complete or partial reversals 
are recorded by WB 1614, 1914, 21 14,2214, 2614, and 2914. Symbols and labels as in Fig. 4, except that numbers here are 
temperatures ("C). 
to rule out CRM overprinting, since the reversal 
temperature corresponds to the Curie temperature of 
magnetite. The N remanence could be a hematite CRM 
resulting from oxidation and would therefore be younger 
than the R magnetization. Note that this mechanism 
does not necessarily require a field reversal between the 
times that R and N were imprinted: CRM could have 
formed anti-parallel to the parent TRM. 
The behaviour of WB 2614 (site 7) is unique in the 
collection. Two successive R magnetizations of slightly 
different orientations (these were averaged in Fig. 6) 
reverse almost 180" to a smaller N magnetization with 
350°C < TB < 625°C (Fig. 7). A pyrrhotite-magnetite 
+ hematite self-reversal or CRM-TRM combination is 
probable. 
The best evidence that a field reversal occurred comes 
from samples of the interior of the intrusion (sites 8 and 
11). WB 2914 and 3114 from site 8 undergo double 
NRM reversals (Figs. 6,7): N (1 15°C < TB < 255OC) -t 
R (255°C < TB < 450°C) + N (450°C < TB < 600°C). 
WB 4214 and 4614 from site 11 record the complete N 
+ R reversal, but the R -t N swing is incomplete 
and obscured by noise. 
What caused these double NRM reversals? A double 
self-reversal is improbable. TRM + two generations of 
CRM is not ruled out, but is unlikely because the 
reversal temperatures, 255 and 450°C, do not correspond 
to Curie points of any common magnetic minerals. 
Furthermore, thermal decay curves of NRM intensity 
for 2914 and most other samples have no marked 
inflection near 300°C. Neither reversal can therefore be 
attributed, even indirectly, to pyrrhotite. 
The likeliest sequence of events is the following. The 
interior of the Wabigoon gabbro cooled slowly enough 
to record two field reversals, at temperatures around 450 
and 250°C. (Properly speaking, all laboratory TB'S 
should be scaled down, using the methods of Pullaiah et 
a1. (1975) or Dodson and McClelland-Brown (1980), to 
allow for the effect of slow cooling.) The margin of the 
intrusion cooled rapidly and recorded only one field 
reversal (or possibly none, if the N remanence is a 
CRM) . 
The reversal record from the reheated contact rocks at 
site 5 is not simple. WB 1714 and 1814 have non- 
reversing NRM's, one of each polarity. WB 1914 
completes a reversal by 500°C, unlike gabbro samples at 
or near the contact whose swings are not complete until 
575580°C. Factors other than cooling history-per- 
haps physicochemical changes resulting from intrusion 
of the gabbr-must govern the reversal record at this 
site. 
Averge directions 
Sample-mean and site-mean magnetization directions 
are plotted in Fig. 8 for 29 stably magnetized samples 
from 11 sites. The characteristic remanence was isolated

by AF cleaning; thermally cleaned results were not used 
in the averaging. The other 26 samples were either 
weakly and unstably magnetized (NRM's usually < 
lo-' emu cm3 A m-I)), lightning struck (a 
particular problem with island and lakeshore sites), or so 
heavily overprinted by PEF remanence that the charac- 
teristic could not be isolated. Site 2 (greenstone 0.25 km 
from the contact) and site 12 had no stably magnetized 
samples, and sites 7 and 11 had only a single stable 
sample each. 
The site 6,7, and 11 means deviate markedly from the 
grand mean (Fig. 8b). However, these "deviant" direc- 
tions are shared by a number of samples from other sites 
(Fig. 8a). The real problem is large dispersion among 
sample means at a given site, making it difficult to obtain 
a representative site mean if there are only one or two 
stable samples. 
AF cleaned data are summarized in Table 1. The R 
directions corresponding to N results were used in 
averaging. The large within-site dispersion is reflected 
in rather low k values for site means and the low 
precision of the grand mean when sample data are 
averaged (k = 9.3) compared with the precision when 
site means are averaged (k = 19.5). Excluding data from 
sites 6,7, and 11 improves the precision of the site-mean 
average (k increases from 19.5 to 47.21, as expected 
from Fig. 8b, but has an insignificant effect on the 
sample-mean average (k changes from 9.3 to 10.1). A k 
of about 10 best represents the scatter of the data. 
However the averaging is done, the mean direction is 
close to D = 240°, I = + lo0, and the corresponding 
paleopole falls near 160°W, 10"s. This pole position fits 
the North American Precambrian apparent polar wander 
path (APWP) (Irving 1979) at either -2800 or - 1250 
Ma. The former implies an Archean age of magnetiza- 
tion for the Wabigoon gabbro. The. latter implies 
remagnetization at the time of the Mackenzie igneous 
episode, whose most obvious expression is the Mackenzie- 
Sudbury dike swarm to the north and the east of the 
Geotraverse area. 
The next section investigates the possibility that the 
Wabigoon dike, whose strike is similar to that of the 
Sudbury dikes, is a member of this swarm, and is 
directly or indirectly responsible for the characteristic 
remanence of the Wabigoon gabbro. 
Results-Wabigoon dike - Dyment greenstone 
Wabigoon dike 
Representative vector magnetization results during 
AF cleaning are depicted in Fig. 9 for sites A and B. Two 
characteristic directions are found. All specimens of 
samples A1 , A3, A4, and A6 have a predominant steep, 
positive, west-directed magnetization, whose mean is 
D = 267.0", I = 79.8" (k = 1997, ag5 = 2.0°, N = 4 
samples) with a virtual geomagnetic pole (VGP) at 
121.5"W, 45.0°N (Sp = 3.8", Sm = 3.9"). At site B, 
both reheated felsic country rocks (sample B1, whose 
0-300 Oe (0-0.03 T) NRM perhaps represents the 
country-rock characteristic remanence) and altered quartz 
diabase dike samples (B2, B3, B4) swing towards this 
direction at AF's of 400-1000 Oe (0.04-0.1 T). 
The VGP of this high-coercivity characteristic rema- 
nence resembles the paleopole of the Abitibi dikes 
(130°W, 41°N; Schutts andDunlop (1981)), for which a 
primary magnetization age of 2150 Ma has been shown 
by a positive contact test and 40Ar/39Ar dating (Hanes 
and York 1979). It also resembles the primary paleopole 
of the 2160 Ma Nipissing diabase (103"W, 42"N; Roy 
and Lapointe (1976); plotted as pole ND7 by Irving 
(1979), Fig. 10) and Irving and McGlynn (198 1, Fig. 
23-10)). 
The second characteristic remanence is a west- 
northwest or east-southeast shallow component exhibited 
by sample A8, taken from a 1 m wide, more felsic dike 
cutting the main dike at site A, and by samples A5 and 
A7, taken within 1-2 m of this subsidiary dike. To 
complicate matters, the NRM of specimen A1 /2 (taken 
far from the small dike) swings to the second characteristic

at 800-1000 Oe (0.08-0.1 T), but the felsic dike 
samples (e.g., A8/2) have NRM's that migrate towards 
the Abitibi-like characteristic above 150 Oe (0.015 T). 
The directional grouping of samples A1 12, A7, and 
A812 is not 180" reversed to the grouping of A5. Neither 
group corresponds closely to any documented Precam- 
brian age of magnetization younger than 2100 Ma and 
older than 1000 Ma, although the A5 grouping is 
perhaps consistent with latest Keweenawan (Halls and 
Pesonen 1982). 
Detailed resampling will be needed to define either 
dike characteristic at an acceptable level of confidence. 
On the preliminary evidence, the dike was probably 
intruded and magnetized about 2100 Ma ago and was 
itself intruded by a minor felsic dike in late Proterozoic 
time (conceivably as late as Grenville time). The 
Wabigoon dike is apparently not of Mackenzie age, and 
likely played no role in the magnetization of the 
Wabigoon gabbro. 
Dyment greenstone 
All specimens of the five Dyment greenstone samples 
cluster about the mean direction, D = 192.8", I = - 14.5" 
(k = 183, ag5 = 5.6"' N = 5 samples). The results are 
plotted in Fig. 10. The corresponding VGP falls at 6YE, 
46.5"N (8p = 2.9", Sm = 5.8"), and is indistinguishable 
from paleopoles for the 2630 Ma Matachewan diabase 
(68"E, 50°N, Irving and Naldrett (1977); 70°E, 45"N, 
Schutts and Dunlop (1981)). 
Site A is evidently too far from the contact to have 
been remagnetized, even partly, by the Wabigoon dike. 
It has, however, been totally remagnetized in latest 
Archean time, presumably as a result of the -2600 Ma 
Kenoran Orogeny. It is worth noting in passing that the 
metavolcanics in the Dyment area deserve further 
detailed study, since they are almost unique among 
greenstones sampled throughout the Geotraverse area in 
possessing reasonably strong (3-20 x lop6 emu cm-3 
or 3-20 X A m-') and stable magnetizations. 
Paleomagnetic poles 
The paleopole for the Wabigoon gabbro (labelled 
WB) and VGP's for the Wabigoon dike (WD) and 
Dyment greenstone (DY) are compared with appropriate 
segments of the Precambrian APWP for North America 
in Fig. 11. Poles and labels in Fig. 11 a follow Halls and 
Pesonen (1982, Fig. 4) for the most part. The remaining 
data follow Irving (1979, Figs. 9-1 I), with additions 
from the recent literature, as noted in the caption. 
DY is indistinguishable from Matachewan diabase 
poles MD and MD2, and is also very similar to the 
-2500 Ma pole PL of the Poohbah Lake complex 
(Dunlop 1979a) of the Quetico gneiss belt (cf. Fig. 1). 
WD is indistinguishable from the Abitibi diabase pri- 
mary pole AD. However, WB is compatible with either 
an Archean age (not necessarily primary) of -2800 Ma 
or a slightly pre-Mackenzie age of - 1300 Ma. Note that 
the oval of confidence for WB in Fig. lla does not 
actually overlap the Mackenzie grouping CP, MX, 
SUD, and MA. WB is possibly consistent with an

### page_10
1814 CAN. J. EARTH XI. VOL. 20. 1983 
FIG. 9. AF-cleaned vector WRM data for specimens of the Wabigoon diabase dike. Symbols and labels as in Fig. 4. 
earliest Keweenawan age, in fact, being intermediate 
between poles S1 and PM2, which have rather large 
confidence ovals. 
Discussion 
The age of pole WB is open to argument. Supporting 
an Archean age is the fact that generally similar poles 
(KK, AB, GR) that have been shown to be pre- 
Matachewan (Irving and Naldrett 1977; Schutts and 
Dunlop 1981) are widespread in the Abitibi volcanic 
subprovince to the east, whereas no - 1300 Ma poles are 
known from the Wabigoon or other volcanic belts of the 
Superior Province. However, the divergence between 
WB and the KK-AB-GR grouping in Fig. 11 b is 
actually just as great as the difference between WB and 
Mackenzieage poles like SUD and MA in Fig. 1 1 a. 
A more compelling argument against -1300 Ma 
remagnetization is the lack of any indication of either 
Elsonian (- 1400 Ma) or Mackenzie (- 1250 Ma) age 
events in the Wabigoon area. To judge by its VGP (WD, 
Fig. 11 b), the Wabigoon dike is of Abitibi (-2150 Ma) 
rather than Mackenzie age. 
Structural arguments are inconclusive. The Wabigoon 
gabbro lies near the axis of an east-west syncline 
passing through Wabigoon Lake. No structural correc- 
tion was made in arriving at pole WB. WB is therefore 
consistent with the -2800 Ma Archean APWP only if 
magnetization postdated folding of the metavolcanics 
and metasediments. However, it is entirely possible that 
intrusion of the Wabigoon body postdated folding, or that 
the entire volcanic-plutonic sequence was remagnetized 
in the late Archean. 
The fact that at least one geomagnetic field reversal 
was apparently recorded during cooling of the Wabigoon 
gabbro at first sight seems to support regional re-

GREEIS TOM 
SITE A 
FIG. 10. AF-cleaned magnetization directions for specimens 
of the Dyment greenstone. All vectors are upward. 
magnetization. Precambrian paleopoles tend to fall in 
groups of predominantly one polarity, implying rather 
infrequent reversals (Robertson and Fahrig 197 1; Halls 
and Pesonen 1982). The probability of recording a 
reversal is therefore much greater if cooling was 
extremely slow, as it would be during regional uplift. 
However, the fact that interior sites record two reversals 
whereas marginal sites record at most one implies that 
the interior cooled slowly compared with the margin. 
This is the pattern expected for initial cooling. 
Unfortunately, a direct contact test of the initial 
cooling hypothesis was unsuccessful. Volcanic rocks at 
site 5 were magnetized in the WB direction, but 
volcanics sampled away from the contact (site 2 and 
seven sites along Highways 17 and 72 in the Dinorwic-

Dyment greenstone was remagnetized in Kenoran times (-2600 Ma); and WB is consistent with a late Archean magnetization 
age of -2800 Ma. 
Wabigoon area) did not yield a stable NRM. Volcanics 
in the Dyment area did behave stably, but had been 
completely remagnetized (to a Kenoran direction) at the 
close of the Archean. 
An alternative approach to dating WB is to determine 
its relative age compared with a superimposed NRM of 
known age. A few Wabigoon samples have a Kenoran- 
type (-2600 Ma) NRM component similar in direction 
to the Dyment overprint (Fig. 10 and VGP DY in Fig. 
llb). Examples are WB 1511, 1711, 1912, 3811 and 
3812 (Fig. 4). In each case, the resultant NRM vector 
migrates from the WB direction towards a southerly, 
shallow, negative vector with progressive AF cleaning. 
The same pattern appears in thermal cleaning (Fig. 6: 
WB 1714, 20-450°C; WB 1914, 20-215"C), but the 
data tend to be noisier and the swings much shorter. 
Only WB 21-4 and 3813 record complete swings that 
allow both vectors in the hybrid NRM to be resolved. 
The simplest interpretation of these swings is that WB 
overprints (and is therefore younger than) the Kenoran 
remanence. Unfortunately this clearcut interpretation 
holds only if it can be shown that WB is a thermal 
overprint, i.e., a partial TRM. The test is the same one 
used earlier to distinguish NRM reversals involving only 
TRM from those due to CRM overprinting TRM, 
namely non-overlap of TB spectra of the two NRM 
components. Unfortunately, the dividing temperature 
between WB and Kenoran NRM's in WB 3813 is 
560-580°C and 21 14 is 500-560°C. In neither case can 
one rule out the possibility that the Kenoran remanence 
is a high-coercivity, high-blocking-temperature hematite 
CRM that overprints the characteristic WB remanence. 
Since there is no evidence for either - 1400 or - 1250 
Ma igneous or metamorphic events in the Wabigoon 
area, is it possible that WB is an 1100-1050 Ma 
overprint that resulted from nearby Keweenawan rifting 
and volcanism? WB is very different from 1100-1050 
Ma paleopoles (Fig. 1 1 a). Suppose, however, that WB 
does not represent a simple univectorial remanence but 
an unresolved bivectorial sum of Keweenawan-age 
NRM and a small Kenoran vector. The bulk of the 
evidence is against such an idea: -Only four samples (WB 
15,17, 19, and 38) show unmistakable swings toward a 
Kenoran direction, and two of these are reheated 
volcanics rather than gabbros. The NRM's of all other 
stable samples approach reasonably well defined WB 
end points and show no signs of migrating towards a 
southerly direction. 
On the other hand, the distribution of sample-mean 
directions is broadly streaked between westerly, steeper, 
positive directions and southwesterly, very shallow 
directions. As Fig. 12 shows, this streaking follows a

### page_12
CAN. J, EARTH SCI. VOL. 20, 1983 
I 
FIG. 12. The distribution of sample-mean Wabigoon gabbro 
magnetizations (Fig. 8a) compared with a great circle joining 
Keweenawan normal directions (Halls and Pesonen 1982, 
Table 2) and Kenoran directions (e.g., MD, PL, DY). The 
three normal-polarity results in Fig. 8a have been reversed in this 
figure. One possible explanation of the streaked distribution 
and high between-sample dispersion is unresolved bivectorial 
(Kenoran + Keweenawan) magnetizations. 
great circle joining Kenoran and Keweenawan normal 
results. If WB actually represents a hybrid of Kenoran 
and Keweenawan remanences, in varying proportions, 
the streaked distribution and resulting high within-site 
scatter would be accounted for in a straightforward way. 
What is not obvious is how AF and thermal demagnetiza- 
tions could fail, in more than 90% of the collection, to 
reveal the composite nature of the remanence. Such 
near-perfect coincidence of the coercivity and blocking- 
temperature spectra of the hypothesized Kenoran and 
Keweenawan remanences seems scarcely credible. 
It must be concluded that most samples of the 
Wabigoon gabbro carry a univectorial remanence but 
are relatively poor and noisy paleofield recorders. 
Conclusion 
A Proterozoic age for the WB characteristic remanence 
is indicated by a straightfomard interpretation of hybrid 
NRM's in the gabbro and its contact rocks. WB has 
lower TB's and coercivities than the Kenoran component 
of NRM; it is therefore likely a younger overprint. It can 
also be argued that in view of the profound effect of the 
Kenoran Orogeny elsewhere in the Geotraverse region, 
it would be unusual if pre-Kenoran magnetizations were 
to have escaped Kenoran overprinting in all but a very 
few Wabigoon samples. 
The evidence against a Proterozoic regional remagnetiza- 
tion is fairly compelling, however. There is no indica- 
tion of a -1300 Ma tectonic or heating event in the 
region. The reversal record of the Wabigoon body 
implies a chilled margin and slowly cooled interior. A 
contact test, which would have settled the question, 
failed because the unbaked country rocks are either 
unstably magnetized or totally reset by the Kenoran 
Orogeny . 
On the basis of this evidence, it is tentatively 
concluded that the Wabigoon gabbro was intruded into 
already folded greenstones in late Archean time and has 
retained a characteristic remanence that largely escaped 
remagnetization in the Kenoran event. The geomagnetic 
field must have reversed fairly frequently at this time, in 
contrast to the situation during much of the Proterozoic, 
since two reversals were recorded during cooling of this 
rather small (1 ?h krn X 5 km) body.
